rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Transitive verbs predominate because a verb can describe either its agent or its object, while every verb requires an agent.
rows.anchor: فكما لا بد للفعل من الفاعل، فكذلك كثر المتعدي

rows.speaker: يحيى بن يعمر، ابن أبي إسحاق، أبو السمال
rows.claim: These readers are cited for a variant pronunciation of the plural waw in اشتروا; the waw has three dialectal vowels, with damma most common, then kasra, then fatha.
rows.anchor: قراءة يحيى بن يعمر3 وابن أبي إسحاق وأبي السمال4

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Damma best marks the plural waw apart from the waw in أو and لو, though some also use damma in لو and some Arabs give the plural waw kasra by analogy.
rows.anchor: لأنها واو جمع، فأرادوا الفرق بينها وبين واو "أو" و"لو"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatha is least common because it is light beside the heavy waw and suffices to separate adjacent quiescent sounds; similar dialectal forms include قم الليل and قل الحق.
rows.anchor: وأما الفتح فأقلها، والعذر فيه خفة الفتحة مع ثقل الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some dialects hamza the waw in forms such as اشترءوا; Ibn Jinni treats this as a weak analogy that gives a temporary vowel the status of a permanent one.
rows.anchor: ينبغي أن يكون ذلك على إجراء غير اللازم مجرى اللازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When hesitating at a pause, speakers lengthen a final vowel and may create a matching glide, as in اشتروا, اشتروي, or اشتروا after the three waw vowels.
rows.anchor: ولو وقفت مستذكرا وقد ضمت الواو؛ لقلت: اشترووا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، الحسن، يحيى بن يعمر، عاصم الجحدري، أبو رجاء
rows.claim: They read وإله أبيك with the singular form of أب, which Abu al-Fath interprets collectively as referring to Jacob's forefathers.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن عباس والحسن ويحيى بن يعمر وعاصم الجحدري وأبي رجاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abīk can be a sound plural of أب meaning forefathers; the following names appose a plural, so this reading needs no forced singular-for-plural interpretation.
rows.anchor: "أبيك" جمع أب على الصحة، على قولك للجماعة: هولاء أبون أحرار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He objects to the phrase بمثل ما آمنتم به because God has no likeness and recommends بما آمنتم به instead.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس: أنه قال: لا تقرأ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report says Ibn Abbas read بالذي آمنتم به; a report associated with the codices of Anas, Abu Salih, and Ibn Masud has بما آمنتم به.
rows.anchor: قال: وروى عنه أيضا أنه كان يقرأ: "بالذي آمنتم به"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas's explanation is sound, but the familiar مثل is not rejected: Arabic uses it emphatically, so the sense remains that they believe as the believers do.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي ذهب إليه ابن عباس حسن؛ لكن ليس لأن القراءة المشهورة مردودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Omitting a recoverable object can make speech more graceful; in وجد من دونهم امرأتين تذودان, the omitted object is their camels, and poetry likewise leaves objects understood.
rows.anchor: أي: تذودان إبلهما، ولو نطق بالمفعول لما كان في عذوبة حذفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-Rumma's description praises balanced speech: its edges neither spill into rambling nor become too spare for what listeners need.
rows.anchor: رخيم الحواشي؛ أي: لا تنتشر حواشيه فتهرأ فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line خير الحديث ما كان لحنا means speech may be deliberately oblique, not grammatically faulty; the Prophetic phrase ألحن بحجته means more adept at arguing a case.
rows.anchor: وليس من اللحن الذي هو إفساد الإعراب، ذلك حديث غير هذا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Via Isa ibn Maymun, al-Hasan reads عشا as people blinded by weeping, deriving it from عَشاة with its feminine ending omitted; Abu al-Fath calls this weak because one day's crying would not blind them.
rows.anchor: ما رواه عيسى بن ميمون عن الحسن أنه قرأ: "وجاءوا أباهم عشا يبكون"

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، الحسن، الضحاك، محمد بن علي، جعفر بن محمد، عمرو بن فائد، يعقوب
rows.claim: They read من كل ما سألتموه with tanwin, making the object explicit: God gave what they asked Him to grant from it; the standard genitive construction leaves the object understood as a share from every kind.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن عباس والحسن والضحاك ومحمد بن علي وجعفر بن محمد

rows.speaker: الجحدري، الثقفي، أبو الهجهاج
rows.claim: They read وأجنبني with hamza; the author explains both جنبني and أجنبني as turning Abraham and his children away from worshipping idols, with the latter also suggesting making them devoted to God.
rows.anchor: قراءة الجحدري والثقفي وأبي الهجهاج: "وأجنبني"3 بقطع الألف

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب، أبو جعفر محمد بن علي، جعفر بن محمد، مجاهد
rows.claim: They read تهوى with fatḥa on the waw, understanding it as love or inclination toward Mecca's people; the standard kasra means to incline toward them, and the variant uses إلى by sense.
rows.anchor: قراءة علي بن أبي طالب وأبي جعفر محمد بن علي وجعفر بن محمد -عليهم السلام- ومجاهد: "تهوى"

rows.speaker: مسلمة بن عبد الله
rows.claim: He is reported to read تهوى إليهم; the author explains the standard تهوي as loving and inclining toward them, supported by the Arabic idiom for a camel that settles down.
rows.anchor: مسلمة بن عبد الله: "تهوى إليهم".

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو، عيسى الثقفي
rows.claim: They read وهنا على وهن with fatḥa on both hāʾs; the author allows وَهَن to be a verbal noun, by analogy with وَضَر and وَحَر.
rows.anchor: الحلواني عن شباب عن أحمد بن موسى عن أبي عمرو وعيسى الثقفي

rows.speaker: الحسن، أبو رجاء الجحدري، قتادة، يعقوب
rows.claim: They read وفصله instead of وفصاله. Faṣl is broader than weaning, while faṣāl better fits this nursing context; the author relates both to separation and cessation.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك قراءة الحسن بخلاف وأبي رجاء الجحدري وقتادة ويعقوب

rows.speaker: عبد الكريم الجزري
rows.claim: He reads فتكن with kasra on kāf, from a bird settling in its nest or roost; the author links the root to dwelling and stability and cites poetry about birds in their nests.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك قراءة عبد الكريم الجزري1:

rows.speaker: يحيى بن عمارة
rows.claim: He reads وأصبغ; the author says ṣād replaces the original sīn under the influence of the following emphatic ghayn, like صقر for سقر and صطر for سطر.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك قراءة يحيى بن عمارة: "وأصبغ عليكم نعمه ظاهرة وباطنة"

rows.speaker: أبو السمال
rows.claim: He reads والسماء رفعها with nominative السماء, making a full nominal sentence coordinated with والنجم والشجر يسجدان; the common accusative instead coordinates on يسجدان with an understood verb رفع.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو السمال: "والسماء رفعها1"، رفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against Abu al-Hasan's ban on coordinating clauses with unlike syntactic positions, Abu al-Fath argues an unspoken case position has no force; he supports this with the accusative reading and analogous omitted pronouns.
rows.anchor: كما أن الضمير في اسم الفاعل لما لم يظهر إلى اللفظ جرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For بالهدى, readers use full tafkhim, imāla, or an intermediate sound: tafkhim keeps the original articulation, while imāla brings the emphatic consonant toward yāʾ; Hamza distinguishes yāʾ-final from wāw-final forms.
rows.anchor: فأما حمزة فأمال ذوات الياء وفخم ذوات الواو ليفرق بين المعنيين

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir lengthens the pronoun hāʾ with a glide, using yāʾ after kasra and waw after damma; other readers indicate its vowel without adding a letter to avoid adjacent consonants around the weak hāʾ.
rows.anchor: ابن كثير باشباع كسرة الهاء ووصلها بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic readily adapts foreign names when Arabized, a point relevant to the name Ibrahim and its variant forms.
rows.anchor: اتساع العرب في الأسماء الأعجمية اذا عربتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وصى and أوصى are both read; they differ as Form II and Form IV verbs, a distinction the author says he explained earlier.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالتشديد من غير ألف وبالتخفيف واثبات الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ reading reports what the speakers said to the Prophet; the tāʾ reading keeps the direct address flowing from أتحاجوننا through أم تقولون to قل أأنتم.
rows.anchor: والحجة لمن قرأ بالتاء أنه عطف باللفظ على معنى الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form with waw and hamza follows a common divine-attribute pattern and can imply an established quality; dropping waw eases the hamza-waw cluster without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: والحجة لمن طرح الواو وهمز أنه مال إلى التخفيف لاجتماع الهمز والواو

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn Amir reads هو مولاها, treating the word as a passive participle used as an object; the other reading موليها has a kasra and takes the subject as the one directing his face toward it.
rows.anchor: قرأه ابن عامر مولاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra in إن تضل makes a conditional clause with a jussive verb; fatḥa in أن تضل treats it as a complement after an understood li, meaning lest one err.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن كسر أنه جعلها حرف شرط وجزم بها تضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فتذكر may be doubled or light and jussive, indicative, or subjunctive: it can continue the conditional, begin a clause after fa, or be governed by the open أن.
rows.anchor: والحجة لمن نصب أنه عطفه على تضل وقد عملت فيه أن المفتوحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading رُهُن is explained as a plural of رهن, while رِهان is also a plural of رهن; the author notes that رهن and سقف are rare plurals on this pattern.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن ضم أنه جمع رهنا رهانا وجمع رهانا رهنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled nūn in أتحاجونني comes from the indicative nūn plus the object nūn before yāʾ, assimilated together; the lighter reading drops one nūn to avoid the pair, as in poetry and تبشرون.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن شدد أن الأصل فيه أتحاجونني بنونين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For وقد هدان, imāla is justified because the form derives from yāʾ and preserves that origin after the pronoun suffix; tafkhim follows the surface form.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى ﴿ وقد هدان ﴾ يقرأ بالإمالة والتفخيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: جذوة has dialectal kasra, fatḥa, and damma forms, with kasra the most eloquent; it means a piece of wood with fire at its end.
rows.anchor: والكسر أفصح ومعنى الجذوة عود في رأسه نار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الرهب may mean fear; Moses feared the staff after it became a serpent, so he was told to press his hand to his ribs to calm himself.
rows.anchor: فقيل هن لغات ومعناهن الفزع والجناح من الإنسان اليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative gloss takes الرهب to mean a sleeve or pocket; on that reading its hāʾ need not be quiescent, since Arabic can reduce originally rounded or fronted vowels.
rows.anchor: وقيل الرهب ها هنا الكم تقول العرب أعطني ما في رهبتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ترجعون is read with tāʾ or yāʾ, following the author’s treatment of similar forms elsewhere; the person shifts between direct address and third-person report.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالتاء والياء على ما قدمناه من القول في أمثاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لنبوئنهم with bāʾ means settle them in chambers, supported by 2:8; the thāʾ form means lodge them, supported by the description of Moses as ثاويا in Midian.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن قرأ بالنون والباء أنه أراد لننزلنهم من الجنة غرفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on the lām in وليتمتعوا marks a threatening imperative; kasra can mark the same lām after waw or a purpose clause coordinated with ليكفروا.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن أسكن أنه جعلها لام وعيد في لفظ الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining readers retain the hamza in connected reading and retain it at pause as well.
rows.anchor: والباقون يصلون بالهمز ويقفون كما يصلون بالهمز

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الدوري، نصير بن يوسف النحوي
rows.claim: They report that al-Kisai imālates طغيانهم and آذانهم; other readers open them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمرو الدوري ونصير بن يوسف النحوي كان الكسائي يميل الألف

rows.speaker: أبو الحارث الليث بن خالد
rows.claim: A conflicting report says al-Kisai does not imālate these forms or their like; the rest read with fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الحارث الليث بن خالد وغيره كان الكسائي لا يميل هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All agree on damma for the plural waw in اشتروا; the disagreement is in the imāla of بالهدى.
rows.anchor: ﴿ اشتروا ﴾ بضم الواو باتفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafi has an intermediate reading on yāʾ-final forms; Qalun and Warsh support it, though al-Musayyibi reports that Nafi opens them throughout, as Ibn Kathir does.
rows.anchor: والأول قول قالون وورش عن نافع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Amr uses an intermediate sound when the form ends an āya, but opens it elsewhere; feminine forms such as الدنيا and شتى remain between opening and imāla.
rows.anchor: فإذا لم يكن رأس آية فتح مثل

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Reports give different pronunciations of أرنا and أرني: one describes a sound between kasra and sukūn, while al-Khaffaf and Abu Zayd report Abu Amr with a quiescent rāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقال الخفاف وأبو زيد عن أبي عمرو ﴿ وأرنا ﴾ بإسكان الراء

rows.speaker: عبد الوارث، اليزيدي، هارون الأعور، عبيد بن عقيل، علي بن نصر
rows.claim: They transmit أرنا and أرني between kasra and sukūn, avoiding either fully marked form.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الوارث واليزيدي وهرون الأعور وعبيد بن عقيل وعلي بن نصر

rows.speaker: نافع، ابن عامر
rows.claim: Nafi and Ibn Amir read وأوصى with the additional alif, while the other readers have وصى.
rows.anchor: فقرأ نافع وابن عامر / وأوصى بهآ /

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، عاصم عن أبي بكر، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers use yāʾ in يقولون; Ibn Amir, Hamza, al-Kisai, and Hafs from Asim use tāʾ in تقولون.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر وأبو عمرو بالياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، حفص عن عاصم، ابن عامر
rows.claim: They read لرؤوف with waw and hamza; other named readers use the lighter form without the waw, while a Kisai transmission from Abu Bakr has a doubled form.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وحفص عن عاصم ﴿ لرؤوف ﴾ على وزن لرعوف

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn Amir reads هو مولها with fatḥa on lām; the other readers read موليها with kasra.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن عامر وحده / هو مولها /

rows.speaker: ورش عن نافع
rows.claim: Some transmissions from Warsh say he leaves the hamza out of لئلا, though many Warsh students do not recognize this; other reports from Nafi and the remaining readers retain the hamza.
rows.anchor: وروى يونس بن عبد الأعلى عن ورش وسقلاب عن ورش عن نافع أنه كان لا يهمز ﴿ لئلا ﴾

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr alone reads ترجعون فيه with fatḥa on tāʾ and kasra on jīm; the other readers use the passive form with ḍamma on tāʾ and fatḥa on jīm.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو عمرو وحده ﴿ ترجعون فيه ﴾ بفتح التاء وكسر الجيم

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Hamza alone reads إن تضل with kasra and فتذكر with doubled kāf and indicative ending; the others use open أن and a subjunctive verb, except Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr, who lighten the verb.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة وحده ﴿ أن تضل ﴾ بكسر الألف ﴿ فتذكر ﴾ بتشديد الكاف ورفع الراء

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: Asim alone reads إلا أن تكون تجارة حاضرة with both words accusative; the other readers use nominative, though Abu Bakr hesitates about Ibn Amir.
rows.anchor: فقرأ عاصم وحده ﴿ إلا أن تكون تجارة حاضرة ﴾ نصبا

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، أبو عمرو، نافع، عاصم، حمزة، الكسائي، ابن عامر
rows.claim: The readers vary in فرهان: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr use the form without alif, with differing reports on hāʾ voweling; Nafi, Asim, Hamza, al-Kisai, and Ibn Amir read رهان with kasra and alif.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي وابن عامر ﴿ فرهان ﴾ بكسر الراء والألف

rows.speaker: حمزة، عاصم عن يحيى بن آدم عن أبي بكر، حفص
rows.claim: These transmissions read الذي اؤتمن with a raised, rounded hamza; Abu Bakr says that notation is not valid Arabic, and another Hamza transmission is likewise called erroneous unless the hamza is quiescent.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة وعاصم في رواية يحيى بن آدم عن أبي بكر وحفص عنه ﴿ الذي اؤتمن ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author declares the quiescent hamza reading the only correct form and rejects the rounded or vowel-signaled hamza variants.
rows.anchor: وهذا خطأ لا يجوز إلا تسكين الهمزة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: They read فيغفر and يعذب in the jussive; Asim and Ibn Amir read both verbs in the indicative.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي ﴿ فيغفر لمن يشاء ويعذب من يشاء ﴾ جزما

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، عاصم عن أبي بكر، ابن عامر، أبو عمرو، حفص، الكسائي، حمزة
rows.claim: They differ between plural كتبه and singular كتبه across 2:285 and 66:12: Abu Amr and Hafs use plural in both; al-Kisai and Hamza use singular in both; others vary by verse or transmission.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو ههنا وفي التحريم ﴿ وكتبه ﴾ جمعا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr lightens the sīn in plural forms attached to a two-letter pronoun, such as رسلنا and رسلكم; a report has him lighten على رسلك, but another says he reads it heavy, as do the other readers generally.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو عمرو ما أضيف إلى مكني على حرفين مثل ﴿ رسلنا ﴾

rows.speaker: عاصم عن أبي بكر، ابن عامر، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: These readers give rāʾ and hamza kasra in رأى; readings before a following quiescent consonant vary by reader and transmission, with full fatḥa, mixed vowels, and in one report kasra on both.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم فى رواية أبى بكر وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائى / رءا / بكسر الراء والهمزة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، أبو عمرو، عاصم، حمزة، الكسائي، نافع، ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisai read أتحاجوني with a doubled nūn; Nafi and Ibn Amir use a light nūn.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائى / أتحجونى / و ﴿ تأمروني ﴾ مشددتين

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisai reads هدان with imāla on dāl; the other readers use fatḥa.
rows.anchor: قرأ الكسائى / هدن / ممالة الدال

rows.speaker: نافع، عاصم عن أبي بكر، ابن عامر، حفص، حمزة، الكسائي، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: The readers vary in forms of تذكرون: several traditions use doubling, while Ali ibn Nasr and Hafs report lightening throughout; Hamza and al-Kisai distinguish yāʾ forms from tāʾ forms, with further exceptions in al-Furqan and al-Isra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائى ﴿ يذكرون ﴾ مشددا إذا كان بالياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، عاصم، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: In وأن هذا صراطي, the readers vary the initial hamza, nūn doubling, and yāʾ vowel: Ibn Amir opens the yāʾ without doubling nūn, while Hamza and al-Kisai use kasra on the hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر ﴿ وأن هذا ﴾ مفتوحة الألف موقوفة النون / صرطى / مفتوحة الياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، ابن عامر، حمزة، الباقون
rows.claim: For صراطي, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read sīn, Hamza uses an intermediate ṣād-zāy sound with variant reports, and the others read ṣād.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وابن عامر / سراطى / بالسين

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، ابن عامر، نافع، عاصم، حمزة، الكسائي، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Ṭā Hā has many vowel traditions: Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir open both; Nafi has several reports from open to intermediate or kasra; Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisai use kasra, Abu Amr varies by transmitter, and Hafs has tafkhim.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وابن عامر ﴿ طه ﴾ بفتح الطاء والهاء

rows.speaker: حمزة، ابن سعدان عن إسحق المسيبي
rows.claim: They read لأهله امكثوا with ḍamma on hāʾ in both 20:10 and 28:29; the others use kasra.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة وابن سعدان عن إسحق المسيبى ﴿ لأهله امكثوا ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، أبو عمرو، عاصم، نافع، ابن عامر، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: They differ in إني أنا: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr open the hamza and yāʾ; the other listed readers use kasra on the hamza, with Nafi alone opening the yāʾ and the rest quiescent.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ﴿ إني أنا ﴾ بفتح الألف والياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، عاصم، ابن عامر، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, and Abu Amr read طوى without declension and with ḍamma on ṭāʾ; Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisai decline it. Abu Zayd glosses it as a land.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو ﴿ طوى وأنا ﴾ غير مجراة والطاء مضمومة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، حمزة، الكسائي، عاصم عن أبي بكر، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: The segment reports singular آية for Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisai, and Asim through Abu Bakr; Ali ibn Nasr also transmits a singular form from Abu Amr.
rows.anchor: وروى على بن نصر عن أبى عمرو / ءاية / واحدة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر
rows.claim: They read ونقول with nūn; Nafi, Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisai read ويقول with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر ﴿ ونقول ﴾ بالنون

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، عاصم، ابن عامر، أبو عمرو، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: The yāʾ of يا عبادي is open for Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Asim, and Ibn Amir in both verses, and quiescent for Abu Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisai; Ibn Amir alone opens أرضي.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم وابن عامر ﴿ يا عبادي ﴾ ههنا وفى الزمر 53 بنصب الياء

rows.speaker: عاصم عن يحيى بن آدم وأبي بكر
rows.claim: Some Asim transmissions read يرجعون with yāʾ; the other readers, including Hafs from Asim, read ترجعون with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم فى رواية يحيى بن آدم وابن أبى أمية عن أبى بكر ﴿ يرجعون ﴾ بالياء

rows.speaker: حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisai read لنثوينهم with thāʾ; the remaining readers use لنبوئنهم with bāʾ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة والكسائى / لنثوينهم / بالثاء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، حمزة، الكسائي، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر، عاصم، نافع
rows.claim: The lām in وليتمتعوا is quiescent in reports from Ibn Kathir, Hamza, and al-Kisai and vocalized by Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, and Asim; Nafi transmissions differ between warning and purpose readings.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وحمزة والكسائى ﴿ وليتمتعوا ﴾ بجزم اللام

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafi's transmitters disagree on وليتمتعوا: al-Musayyibi, Qalun, Ismail, and Abu Bakr ibn Abi Uways give the threatening sukūn, while Ibn Jammaz, Ismail ibn Jafar, and Warsh give the purpose reading with kasra.
rows.anchor: واختلف عن نافع فروى المسيبى وقالون وإسماعيل وأبو بكر ابنا أبى أويس

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr pauses on عباد at an āya ending but reads عباد الذين with the yāʾ when the phrase continues; his reading is described as pausal separation.
rows.anchor: وقال عبيد عن أبى عمرو إن كانت رأس آية وقفت ﴿ عباد ﴾

rows.speaker: قنبل عن النبال عن أصحابه عن ابن كثير
rows.claim: Qunbul transmits from Ibn Kathir عبادِ الذين without the yāʾ, with kasra on dāl; the other readers also omit the yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأت على قنبل عن النبال عن أصحابه عن ابن كثير ﴿ عباد ﴾ الذين ) بكسر الدال من غير ياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: They read سلما with alif and kasra on lām; the others use the form without alif and with fatḥa, also reported from Aban for Asim.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ﴿ سلما ﴾ بألف ولام مكسورة

rows.speaker: حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisai read بكاف عبده as a plural; the remaining readers use the singular.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائى ﴿ بكاف عبده ﴾ جماعا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو، عاصم عن الكسائي عن أبي بكر
rows.claim: These readings use tanwin on كاشفات and ممسكات; the others attach ضره and رحمته in a genitive construction.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وعاصم فى رواية الكسائى عن أبى بكر عنه / كشفت ضره / و / ممسكت رحمته / منونا

rows.speaker: حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: They read قضى with ḍamma on qāf, fatḥa on yāʾ, and الموت nominative; the other readers use fatḥa on qāf and accusative الموت.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائى ﴿ قضى ﴾ بضم القاف وفتح الياء ﴿ الموت ﴾ رفعا

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، ابن عامر، عاصم، أبو زيد عن أبي عمرو، حمزة، الكسائي، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Ibn Amir, Asim, and one Abu Amr report open the yāʾ in يا عبادي; Hamza, al-Kisai, and other Abu Amr transmissions leave it quiescent.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وعاصم ﴿ يا عبادي ﴾ محركة الياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر، حفص عن عاصم، عاصم عن أبي بكر، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: The first group reads بمفازتهم in the singular; Asim through Abu Bakr, Hamza, and al-Kisai read it in the plural.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحفص عن عاصم ﴿ بمفازتهم ﴾ واحدة

rows.speaker: نافع، ابن عامر
rows.claim: Nafi and Ibn Amir lighten the nūn in تأمروني; Nafi opens the yāʾ, whereas Ibn Amir does not.
rows.anchor: فقرأ نافع وابن عامر ﴿ تأمروني ﴾ بتخفيف النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant drops hamza from mustahziʾūn; the source calls it the most streamlined form and common in recitation traditions.
rows.anchor: Hamza dropped entirely (canonical in 10-reader system) — most streamlined form, common in recitation traditions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical Form IV awṣā reading replaces Form II waṣṣā, shifting from intensified charging to formal bequeathing while keeping the testament sense.
rows.anchor: Canonical Form IV reading changes waṣṣā to awṣā, shifting from intensified charging to formal bequeathing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrāhāmu is a canonical adaptation of Ibrahim with long ā in the final syllable, affecting pronunciation and lineage resonance rather than syntax.
rows.anchor: Canonical name-form variant with ā in the final syllable; it affects pronunciation and lineage resonance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrāhīma is the standard canonical form, with long ī before final mīm.
rows.anchor: Standard canonical form: Ibrāhīma with long ī before final mīm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrāhāma is a canonical phonological adaptation of the same foreign name, using ā rather than ī before mīm.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with fatḥa + alif (ā) instead of kasra + yāʾ (ī) before mīm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar has a quiescent hāʾ in hwa rather than huwa, a rapid-recitation reduction with no semantic change.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on hāʾ — هْوَ (hwa) instead of هُوَ (huwa)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading in as a conditional yields if one of them errs; an instead makes the phrase purposive, so that or lest one errs. Both are canonical.
rows.anchor: Both are canonical seven readings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form IV tudhkira is a simpler causative than Form II tudhakkira; both are canonical readings with related causative senses.
rows.anchor: Form IV (afʿala) instead of Form II (faʿʿala): tudhkira vs tudhakkira

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indicative ending presents her reminding as an independent fact; the subjunctive makes it a purpose or result. Both are canonical.
rows.anchor: Indicative instead of subjunctive: -u ending vs -a. Changes from purpose/result

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nominative tijāratun makes kāna complete, meaning that a present trade exists, rather than taking an accusative predicate; both are canonical.
rows.anchor: Nominative instead of accusative: tijāratun ḥāḍiratun. Changes kāna from defective verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nominative ḥāḍiratun agrees with the nominative tijāratun reading and the complete-verb analysis of kāna.
rows.anchor: Nominative, matching the tijāratun variant above. Same logic: complete kāna reading

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar and Yaʿqub quiesce the final rāʾ in yuḍār; the source treats it as phonetic, with the same morphological analysis.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on final rāʾ (Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb). Phonetic variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruhun and rihān are both canonical plurals of rahn: the former is broken and the latter sound.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: ruhun (plural of rahn) instead of rihān — both are valid plurals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ of the plural pronoun may have kasra or ḍamma in ilayhum, a dialectal voweling difference with no semantic effect.
rows.anchor: Kasra vs. ḍamma on hāʾ al-jamʿ — dialectal variation in 3rd person plural pronoun voweling

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This entry repeats the ilayhum hāʾ-vowel variant: kasra versus ḍamma is dialectal and does not change meaning.
rows.anchor: Kasra vs. ḍamma on hāʾ al-jamʿ — dialectal variation; identical to word 15 variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ in ʿalayhum likewise varies between kasra and ḍamma without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Kasra vs. ḍamma on hāʾ al-jamʿ — dialectal variation; no semantic difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavy nūn in a-tuḥājjūnnī is presented as the standard reading and adds emphasis to the challenge.
rows.anchor: Heavy nūn (nūn mushaddada) — emphasizes confrontation, standard reading

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light nūn reading a-tuḥājjūnī removes emphasis and softens the confrontational tone.
rows.anchor: Light nūn (nūn mukhaffafa) — drops emphasis, softens the accusatory tone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This variant retains the full yāʾ in hadānī at pause, extending the pronoun for clarity.
rows.anchor: Full yāʾ retained — Ten Readers variant; extends the pronoun for clarity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At pause the form has nūn quiescent, while connected reading retains hadānī; this is a phonetic adaptation.
rows.anchor: Pausal form: nūn sākina at waqf, full -nī in waṣl — phonetic adaptation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imāla tilts the fatḥa on dāl toward kasra without changing the meaning.
rows.anchor: Imāla (vowel tilting): fatḥa on dāl tilted toward kasra — dialectal phonetic variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Form IV yunzil reading contrasts with Form II yunazzil, shifting from gradual sending to a single act; both are canonical.
rows.anchor: Form IV yunzil (anzala) vs standard Form II yunazzil (nazzala) — shifts from gradual/staged sending

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilating tāʾ into dhāl simplifies tatadhakkarūna to tadhdhakkarūna without changing meaning; the heavier cluster may echo active remembrance.
rows.anchor: Full assimilation of tāʾ into dhāl (tadhdhakkarūna from tatadhakkarūna) — phonological simplification

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inna with kasra makes an independent emphatic assertion, rather than the subordinate clause anna; Hamza and al-Kisai read this form.
rows.anchor: Inna (with kasra) instead of anna (with fatḥa) — changes from subordinate clause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light an with quiescent nūn is a masdariyya particle rather than emphatic inna, changing syntactic weight but not the core sense.
rows.anchor: Light an (with sukūn on nūn) instead of anna (with shadda) — masdariyya particle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Amir opens the possessive yāʾ in ṣirāṭiya instead of leaving it quiescent; the fuller pronunciation does not change meaning.
rows.anchor: Fat-ḥa on the yāʾ (ṣirāṭiya) instead of sukūn (ṣirāṭī) — fuller pronunciation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qunbul from Ibn Kathir reads sīn instead of ṣād in sirāṭī, a phonological substitution for the same root.
rows.anchor: Sīn replaces ṣād — phonological variant (ibdāl); Qunbul from Ibn Kathīr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalaf from Hamza gives ṣād an intermediate pronunciation with ishmām of zāy.
rows.anchor: Ṣād with ishmām of zāy — intermediate pronunciation between ṣ and z

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tāʾ assimilates into the following tāʾ in fa-ttafarraqa; this is articulatory and does not change meaning.
rows.anchor: Assimilation of tāʾ — phonological variant with tāʾ assimilated into the following tāʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lighter mayt reading drops yāʾ gemination; some grammarians distinguish mayt as already dead from mayyit as dying or recently dead.
rows.anchor: Vowel reduction: mayyiti → mayti — dropping the shaddah (gemination) on yāʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the same reduction in the accusative form: mayyita becomes mayta by dropping yāʾ gemination.
rows.anchor: Same vowel-reduction variant as word 18 — mayyita → mayta, dropping gemination on yāʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard reading retains the hamza in al-dhiʾbu.
rows.anchor: Standard reading with hamza: al-dhiʾbu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A tashīl form drops the hamza and lengthens the preceding vowel, producing al-dhību.
rows.anchor: Tashīl/hamza-dropping variant: al-dhību (hamza elided, compensatory lengthening

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In pause, al-dhīb ends with sukūn; connected reading uses al-dhiʾbu.
rows.anchor: Waqf (pause) variant: al-dhīb with sukūn; read in connected speech as al-dhiʾbu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun suffix in li-ahlihu has ḍamma instead of kasra; the source suggests dialectal leveling or a different syntactic analysis.
rows.anchor: Nominative -hu instead of genitive -hi on pronoun suffix; Abu Jaʿfar and others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person yāʾ is open in inniya rather than quiescent in innī, changing prosody without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Open yāʾ (inniya) vs. quiescent yāʾ (innī) — a phonological variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ in laʿalliya is open rather than quiescent, paralleling the inniya variant and leaving the meaning unchanged.
rows.anchor: Open yāʾ (laʿalliya) vs. quiescent yāʾ (laʿallī) — phonological variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In li-ahlihu the pronoun suffix shifts from kasra to ḍamma, a minor phonetic variant of the third-person masculine pronoun.
rows.anchor: Hū-iḍāfa variant: the pronoun suffix vowel shifts from -i (standard harmony after kasra) to -u

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This bundled entry links the preceding pronoun-vowel shift to the juncture with the imperative's hamzat al-waṣl.
rows.anchor: Same vhr entry in bundle — the preceding pronoun's vowel shift affects the juncture

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person possessive yāʾ in inniya takes fatḥa instead of sukūn, a prosodic variant with identical meaning.
rows.anchor: Y-iḍāfa variant: the 1st-sg pronoun yāʾ takes fatḥa instead of sukūn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ in laʿalliya takes fatḥa, parallel to the same yāʾ-fatḥa pattern in inniya, with no semantic shift.
rows.anchor: variant: same yāʾ-fatḥa pattern

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judhwatin has damma on the first radical, an alternate vocalization of jadhwa; the source says dictionaries attest all three vowels.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant: damma on the first radical — judhwa alternative form of jadhwa

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jidhwatin has kasra on the first radical and is listed as a synonym of jadhwa, with a slight nuance toward a stump.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant: kasra on the first radical — jidhwa variant; classical dictionaries list as synonym

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive third-person plural shifts from direct address to a narrative statement about people being returned.
rows.anchor: Third person plural passive — shifts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active Form I means you return, making the audience the grammatical agent rather than the recipient of passive return.
rows.anchor: passively; agency shifts to audience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The th-w-y reading emphasizes taking up long residence in the chambers rather than the act of settlement associated with b-w-ʾ.
rows.anchor: From th-w-y (to reside/dwell): canonical variant shifts root from b-w-ʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This hamza-removal form keeps the b-w-ʾ root and is semantically identical to the standard reading.
rows.anchor: Hamza-removal variant of the standard: same root b-w-ʾ but without hamza

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard form uses the emphatic heavy nūn, with a third-person plural subject.
rows.anchor: Standard reading with emphatic nūn thaqīla (heavy nūn of emphasis)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A light nūn reduces emphasis but preserves the prohibition's meaning.
rows.anchor: Light nūn (nūn khafīfa) replaces heavy nūn — reduced phonetic emphasis

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bunay has sukūn on the final yāʾ, a shorter and more compressed diminutive form.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on final yāʾ: bunay — a shorter diminutive form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bunayyi has kasra on the final yāʾ, making the possessive marking more explicit.
rows.anchor: Kasra on final yāʾ: bunayyi — the possessive yāʾ (ī) is partially retained

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final nūn changes from kasra to ḍamma in anu, described as phonetic assimilation before the imperative.
rows.anchor: Vowel change on final nūn: kasra (ani) → ḍamma (anu) — phonetic assimilation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bunay has sukūn on the final yāʾ, shortening the diminutive and lightening its pronunciation.
rows.anchor: Shortened form with sukūn on final yāʾ — removes the tashdīd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bunayyi retains kasra on the final yāʾ, which the source treats as a grammatical variant with more explicit possessive inflection.
rows.anchor: Kasra on final yāʾ (bunayyi) — genitive/possessive inflection made explicit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form II jammaʿa intensifies gathering, suggesting persistent or excessive accumulation rather than a single act; both Forms I and II are canonical.
rows.anchor: Form II intensive jamma'a (gemination of middle radical) — intensifies the gathering

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaḥsibu with kasra on sīn is a canonical variant of yaḥsabu with fatḥa; both mean he supposes and differ only in vocal pattern.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with kasra on the sin (yaḥsibu vs yaḥsabu). Both are mutawatir readings
